idiom_name: proxy class overriding __getattribute__/__setattr__/__delattr__ + WeakKeyDictionary identity map
implementation_notes: Python has no interception hook beyond the attribute protocol: __getattr__ runs only after normal lookup fails, while __getattribute__ is called for every attribute access (datamodel), so the membrane is a proxy class overriding __getattribute__/__setattr__/__delattr__ whose returned attributes are wrapped - methods are wrapped in a function that wraps arguments and results. The identity map is a WeakKeyDictionary (or WeakValueDictionary for the other direction) so one target yields one proxy without being pinned, and revocation is a flag checked in the wrapper. The whole structure is hand-written; the classic form is justified when a mediated object graph must survive calls in both directions, while a decorator over one function or a narrow explicit interface is enough when a single operation crosses the boundary.
pitfalls: __getattr__ is not __getattribute__: it fires only after normal lookup fails, so a proxy that defines only __getattr__ silently exposes its own attributes (and anything the proxy shares with the target) - total mediation needs __getattribute__.

Special methods are looked up on the type, not the instance: __add__, __iter__, __enter__ and friends must be defined on the proxy class itself, since __getattribute__ cannot intercept operators or protocol dispatch.
The identity map must be weakly keyed and the proxy must not strongly reference the target through the map's values, or the map pins the wrapped graph; plain dicts leak.
Every intercepted access costs a Python frame and isinstance/type checks see the proxy, not the target, unless __class__ is spoofed deliberately.

variants.name: wrapt.ObjectProxy subclass (library-assisted transparency)
variants.idiom_name: class MembraneProxy(wrapt.ObjectProxy) overriding only the mediated members
variants.implementation_notes: The wrapt package provides a transparent object proxy: ObjectProxy passes attribute access through to the wrapped object, exposes it as __wrapped__, and handles the awkward parts of transparency (slots, descriptors, __class__ reporting) in a C extension, so a membrane only overrides the members it must mediate and calls self.__wrapped__ for the rest (wrapt documentation). That inverts the usual trade-off: less code to write, but the mediated surface is exactly the overridden set, so un-overridden members remain raw routes, and the membrane now depends on a third-party package. Use it when the mediation is selective (log or attenuate a handful of calls) and the surrounding stack already depends on wrapt - instrumentation, mocking and AspectJ-style libraries do; use the dunder-proxy variant when the interior of the wrapper must be fully controlled or dependencies must stay stdlib-only.
pitfalls: Only overridden members are mediated: like Kotlin's `by`, ObjectProxy forwards everything else transparently, so the mediated surface is what you explicitly write and nothing warns about the rest.
Names starting with _self_ are stored on the proxy rather than forwarded; anything else lands on the wrapped object through __setattr__, which is a silent way to write through the membrane.

The dependency and the C extension are part of the trust base now: a security boundary that relies on wrapt must pin and audit it, and the proxy still cannot intercept operators unless they are defined on the subclass.
